candidates.title: Draft an agent recovery checklist

demandEvidence.chore: Developers must write checkpointing and recovery logic and handle idempotency for agents.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: But devs need to write checkpointers, recovery logic, and deal with idempotency by theirselves.

experimentPlan.output: A draft recovery checklist for one operator-described agent failure, covering saved state, retry behavior, and duplicate-action risk.
inputs: Synthetic agent task and failure point
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits one fictional or sanitized agent failure scenario for review.
steps: Collect the failure point and last known saved state.
Ask the operator which actions may have side effects.
Draft checkpoint and retry questions from the supplied details.
Flag where repeated actions could cause duplicates.
Return a checklist for an engineer to review and edit.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a small set of fictional scenarios, check that each draft repeats the supplied failure point and flags the operator-marked side effect without inventing a recovery action.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: An engineer supplies system details, verifies all suggested checks, writes and tests recovery logic, and authorizes any production change.
unverified: No supplied implementation source documents agent checkpointing or idempotency mechanics.
The source does not establish how often this chore occurs or who would buy a service.
The proposed drafting workflow has not been implemented or tested.

ease.reason: A beginner can organize a fictional failure scenario, but no supplied source supports the recovery mechanics; an engineer must validate the checklist.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: agent developers or consultants might pay for recovery planning; this single question establishes no buying intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week draft-only test is bounded, but correct checkpoints and side-effect handling depend on system details not supplied here.

autonomy.reason: The tool could structure supplied details, but an engineer must design, test, and approve every real recovery action; mechanics are unsupported.

evidence.reason: The fresh post explicitly names checkpointers, recovery logic, and idempotency as developer work, but gives no example, recurrence, or corroboration.

candidates.reason: Concrete developer chores support a narrow checklist experiment, but unsupported implementation mechanics and unverified buyer demand leave the provisional mean below 6.

candidates.title: Flag repeat processing after missed triggers

demandEvidence.chore: Review lead records processed again after a missed schedule trigger to identify possible duplicates.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Missed schedule triggers can duplicate everything.

experimentPlan.output: A review file that flags repeated synthetic lead records across two submitted batches for a human to inspect.
inputs: Expected duplicate pairs for a small test set
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits two sample batches after describing a possible repeat-processing event.
steps: Read only the operator-selected test fields.
Compare rows using the proposed matching rule.
Mark likely repeated rows and show which fields matched.
Produce a review list without deleting or changing records.
Ask an operator to confirm each match and refine the rule.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: For a hand-labeled synthetic set, compare flagged pairs with the supplied expected pairs and record false matches and missed pairs before any live use is considered.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A workflow operator chooses safe fields, checks every flagged pair, and handles schedule configuration or record changes; no live system is connected in this proposal.
unverified: No supplied reference documents n8n schedule triggers or duplicate suppression.
The selected spans do not specify record fields, matching rules, frequency, or outcomes.
The proposed mock and customer interest have not been tested.

ease.reason: A beginner can compare synthetic batches in a review mock, but the spans give no matching fields and no source supports trigger behavior.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: lead-generation workflow consultants might pay to reduce repeat processing; the post does not establish buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic comparison is bounded, while reliable matching and schedule recovery need unprovided fields and workflow access.

autonomy.reason: A proposed comparison can flag likely repeats, but an operator must confirm matches and manage the trigger; execution is unsupported.

evidence.reason: One retained task span states that missed schedule triggers can duplicate processing; frequency, fields, and corroboration are absent from these spans.

candidates.reason: The retained task span supports this specific bounded mock, but no implementation support or recurrence evidence is supplied; provisional mean is below 6.

candidates.title: Pass received images into reply review

demandEvidence.chore: Provide an already received customer image together with its message to a reply assistant so it need not be requested again.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Even though the image has already been received and downloaded, the AI agent asks the customer to send the image again.

experimentPlan.output: A draft reply-review packet that pairs a fictional customer message with its supplied image description and flags when image context is missing.
inputs: Operator-written description of a fictional image
Expected product description or missing-context label
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits a synthetic message and its paired image description for a routing review.
steps: Store the message and image description as one test case.
Check that both fields are present in the same packet.
Draft a short product-identification question only when the supplied description is insufficient.
Show the packet and draft to a human reviewer.
Compare the draft with the expected test label and revise the prompt.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Across fictional paired and unpaired examples, verify the packet preserves the correct pairing and does not claim to inspect an image when only a description was supplied.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A person supplies test descriptions, checks all product interpretations and replies, and authorizes any real Messenger integration or message; no customer images are used in this proposal.
unverified: No supplied reference documents Make routing, Messenger access, image transfer, or image analysis.
The post describes one troubleshooting request and does not establish how often it occurs or buyer intent.
The proposed packet workflow has not been executed in Make or tested with images.

ease.reason: A paired synthetic-input mock is manageable, but no supplied source documents Make routing or passing image inputs to an assistant.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: service firms handling product messages might pay to avoid repeated image requests; the question proves no buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic packet test is bounded, while actual Messenger access, image handling, and interpretation remain unsupported.

autonomy.reason: The proposal can assemble test context, but a person must check image interpretation and approve replies; integration is unverified.

evidence.reason: The retained post describes text and image routes and the repeated-image request problem; recurrence and implementation evidence are absent from the supplied source.

candidates.reason: The full retained span supports a specific handoff problem and a bounded mock; the key integration is unsupported and the provisional mean is below 6.

candidates.title: Review booking requests for conflicts

demandEvidence.chore: Check salon booking requests against working hours, provider availability, and existing appointments before confirmation.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: Every booking request checks salon working hours, master availability, and existing appointments in PostgreSQL at the SQL level before confirmation.

experimentPlan.output: A draft conflict-review table for fictional salon booking requests, showing which supplied availability or appointment condition needs a person's check.
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator submits a fictional booking request and matching test calendar records.
steps: Extract the proposed date and time from the supplied test request.
Compare it with the supplied working-hours fixture.
Check the supplied provider availability fixture.
Check the supplied appointment fixture for overlap.
Return a conflict-review table without confirming or writing a booking.
Have a person compare each result with expected labels.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: Use hand-labeled synthetic cases for outside-hours, unavailable-provider, overlapping, and clear slots; compare every flag with the expected label and require human review of errors.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A salon operator must verify the calendar, resolve ambiguous dates, approve any real booking, and review privacy and access before deployment.
unverified: No attached implementation reference supports this booking workflow; the post's described architecture is not independent verification.
The source is a maker's architecture post and does not establish buyer intent or payment.
Synthetic checks do not establish database persistence, concurrency safety, or tax correctness.

ease.reason: A student can lay out fictional conflict cases, but no supplied implementation reference supports calendar checks or safe booking changes.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: salons might pay for fewer booking conflicts; this maker architecture post establishes no buyer intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week synthetic fixture test is bounded, but real calendar access, concurrency handling, and persistence are unverified.

autonomy.reason: The proposal only flags test conflicts; a person must validate availability and confirm bookings, and execution is unsupported.

evidence.reason: Retained spans describe salon requests and a maker-reported validation architecture, but do not establish external demand or independent implementation evidence.

candidates.reason: A bounded conflict-review mock can be scoped from the described booking checks, but this is maker evidence rather than verified buyer demand and the unsupported implementation keeps the provisional mean below 6.

candidates.title: Review duplicate records in a Make workflow

demandEvidence.chore: Diagnose and fix duplicate records being created by a business integration.

experimentPlan.output: A review sheet that flags likely duplicate rows in two operator supplied test batches and shows the fields that matched.
inputs: Two synthetic batches of integration records
Operator selected fields allowed for comparison
experimentPlan.trigger: An operator provides two fictional or sanitized test batches after seeing records appear more than once.
steps: Use only the operator selected comparison fields.
Compare rows across the two supplied batches with a stated matching rule.
List possible duplicate pairs and show the matching fields.
Keep all rows unchanged and produce a review sheet.
Ask a person to confirm each pair and adjust the rule.
experimentPlan.acceptanceCheck: On a hand labeled synthetic set, compare flagged pairs with expected pairs and record false matches and missed pairs; do not change or delete any record.
experimentPlan.humanBoundary: A workflow operator chooses fields, confirms every flagged pair, diagnoses the live scenario, and authorizes any change; this proposal uses no production data or connection.
unverified: No supplied reference documents duplicate matching or prevention in Make.
The post gives no fields, specific case details, frequency, or outcome for the duplicate records.
The Make error handler reference (428eda549e557f199c3af452) documents intercepting module errors, not duplicate detection or repair.
The proposed test and customer interest have not been validated.

ease.reason: A student can compare synthetic records in a simple review sheet, but the supplied Make documentation (428eda549e557f199c3af452) covers module errors, not duplicate matching.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small integration service firms might pay for duplicate-record diagnosis; the discussion indicates a stated need, not buying intent or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can compare hand labeled synthetic rows; choosing reliable fields and diagnosing a real integration remain unverified.

autonomy.reason: A proposed comparison can flag possible repeats, but an operator must confirm matches and implement any fix; the reference (428eda549e557f199c3af452) does not document deduplication.

evidence.reason: The retained span explicitly lists duplicate records as an issue and offers fixed-price help for defined integration problems, but gives no specific case or recurrence.

candidates.reason: The literal chore supports a bounded synthetic comparison experiment. Its score is below six because matching fields, recurrence, and duplicate-fix mechanics are not evidenced.
